1 Faculty Senate February 1, 2006 Faculty Senate Curricular Affairs Committee Four Hundred and Thirty-Ninth Report Proposal for the Establishment of the Department of Physical Therapy as a Separate Academic Department At its meeting of January 31, 2006, The Curricular Affairs Committee approved the following proposal for the establishment of the Department of Physical Therapy as a separate academic department and recommends confirmation by the Faculty Senate. The proposal is in the format required by the Board of Governors for Higher Education. A.GENERAL INFORMATION 1. Name of institution University of Rhode Island 2. Names of administrative units Kinesiology Department College of Human Science and Services 3. Title of proposed organizational unit Physical Therapy Department 4. Intended date of change Upon Board of Governors approval 5. Intended location of organizational unit University of Rhode Island, Kingston Campus

2 6. Institutional review and approval process Approval Date Physical Therapy Program Faculty March 3, 2004 Kinesiology Department April 22, 2004 Human Science & Services Curriculum Committee Sept. 14, 2005 Human Science & Services College Faculty Oct. 19, 2005 Faculty Senate Curricular Affairs Committee January 31, 2006 Faculty Senate February 23, 2006 President of the University March 1, 2006 7. Summary description of the proposed organization change. The purpose of this proposal is to change the standing of the Physical Therapy Program from a program within the Kinesiology Department to a separate Department within the College of Human Science and Services. 8. Signature of the President ______________________________ Robert L. Carothers 9. Resources The organizational changes proposed herein require no new resources. The Physical Therapy Program has its own director, faculty, secretarial support, facilities, and operating budget. 10. Person to be contacted during the review Diane Horm Associate Dean College of Human Science and Services diane@uri.edu 874-2403 Beth Marcoux, PT, PhD Program Director Physical Therapy bmarcoux@mail.uri.edu 874-5627 11. Signed agreements for cooperative arrangements. None

3 B.RATIONALE This organizational change is being proposed because the Physical Therapy Program can better fulfill its mission to educate competent doctors of physical therapy who can provide skilled patient care in a variety of settings, conduct clinical research, and provide service to the community at large if it is an academic department within the College of Human Science and Services rather than a program within the Kinesiology Department.
The mission of the Physical Therapy Program focuses on professional, graduate rather than undergraduate education as is the case in the Kinesiology Department.
There are no common students between the two units nor does faculty teach across the units.
The reorganization will allow PT faculty to focus their efforts on continued development and advancement of the program, clinical and basic science research related to the profession and provision of service to the community and profession.
The Physical Therapy Program has functioned autonomously within the (Department of Physical Education now renamed) Kinesiology Department since its inception in 1991.

It has had its own faculty, support staff, facilities, and budget from the very beginning as a requirement of professional accreditation.
Further, due to accreditation requirements, the Program Director has maintained direct communication with the Dean of the College and was a regular participant at College Management meetings.
A self-study report for the Commission on Accreditation in Physical Therapy Education was recently completed in preparation for a site visit that occurred in September 2005.
It was during this self- evaluation that the faculty recognized that the Program was intended to be a separate entity within the college from its development and that separation would allow for better overall functioning of the program.
With the recent move from the masters of physical therapy to the doctor of physical therapy, the program is even more out of place being located within the Kinesiology Department.
Separation will allow better collaboration between the Physical Therapy Program and other departments such as Communicative Disorders and Biology.

This re- organization will simplify day-to-day operations and clarify evaluation of program activities because data will no longer be combined with that of the Kinesiology department.
Please note that no new resources are needed to affect this organizational change.
C.INSTITUTIONAL ROLE This organizational change is consistent with the published role and mission of URI.
The Department of Physical Therapy will have all of the responsibilities of a Department.
In addition, it will provide added value to the University through its recognition as the only Physical Therapy Program in the state and via the clinic, which provides physical therapy to citizens of Rhode Island.

4 D.INTERINSTITUTIONAL CONSIDERATIONS The projected impact of this organizational change on the other public higher educational institutions in Rhode Island is nil. Other institutions in Rhode Island will not be affected by this change because the Physical Therapy Program is not a new program and is not competing with other programs in the state for students or resources. There are no cooperative arrangements with other institutions relative to this organizational change. E.EVALUATION The Physical Therapy Program is fully accredited through the Commission on Accreditation in Physical Therapy Education (CAPTE). Evaluation of the program is on going and includes both direct and indirect measures of clearly defined outcomes. Examples of outcome measures include the percentage of students who pass the National Physical Therapy Licensure Exam, the percentage of students who receive outstanding grades on the clinical performance instrument, a tool that is used nationally to evaluate the performance of students in the clinical setting, and responses from employers gathered both on surveys and in focus groups. Effective this semester, the PT program will begin using the electronic portfolio system recently purchased by URI called “True Outcomes”. Data from these evaluations will be used to make necessary changes in the doctor of physical therapy degree program.

Summary of Proposed Organizational Change The College of Pharmacy presently consists of three Departments: The Department of Applied Pharmaceutical Science (APS); The Department of Biomedical Science (BMS) and the Department of Pharmacy Practice (PHP). The Department of APS consists of two sections, a Pharmaceutics Section and a Pharmacoepidemiology / Pharmaceconomics Section. During the 2002-2003 academic year the Dean of the College established a committee with representation from all three departments. The committee was charged to consider ways of optimizing the administration, research program and teaching activities of the College. After discussions with the Dean of the College, it was recommended that the College be reorganized into two departments. It was proposed that the Pharmaceutics Section of APS and the whole of BMS should be merged to form a new Department of Biomedical and Pharmaceutical Sciences (BPS). It was further proposed that the Pharmacoepidemiology and Pharmacoeconomics section of APS become part of the Department of PHP. 9. Signature of the President _________________________________ Robert L.
Carothers 11.
Person to Contact During the Review Judith Swift Interim Vice Provost for Academic Programs and Services 874-4408 B.
RATIONALE The College of Pharmacy presently consists of three Departments: The Department of Applied Pharmaceutical Science (APS); The Department of Biomedical Science (BMS) and the Department of Pharmacy Practice (PHP).
Faculty in PHP are primarily clinicians, who are directly involved in patient care and as a result are primarily based at clinical sites throughout the state.
In contrast, faculty in APS and BMS are based at the Kingston campus.
Furthermore, with the exception of the Pharmacoepidemiology and Pharmacoeconomics (PE/PE) Section of APS, the research activities of APS and BMS are primarily laboratory based.
As pharmaceutical science and biomedical science has evolved in the last decade there has been an increasing overlap in the research activities of the two departments.
However, the present departmental structure discourages collaboration and hinders interaction between and among faculty.

The proposed departmental structure would address this problem and hopefully lead to cross-fertilization of research efforts between the two existing departments.
Owing to the more practice oriented research activities of the PE/PE section of APS, a more logical placement for this section would be within the department of PHP.
These organizational changes will also enable the College to address its graduate program and consider ways to make the program more cost-effective and to better prepare the graduates for careers in pharmaceutical and biological science.
The new structure would have minimal effect on the courses offered in College of Pharmacy.
The College of Pharmacy's main teaching responsibility is delivery of the Doctor of Pharmacy curriculum.
Since this is a College-wide integrated curriculum, the proposed restructuring would only lead to some recoding and renumbering of courses.
It is anticipated that the improved communication associated with the proposed changes will enhance the coordination of course content and reduce overlap between courses. 420CAC http://www.uri.edu/facsen/420CAC.html 3 of 4 1/6/14, 5:35 PM

Overall it is anticipated that the proposed re-structuring would: increase collaboration between and among faculty in the College of Pharmacy; promote cross-disciplinary research projects; improve the quality and cost-effectiveness of the graduate program and improve the delivery of the Doctor of Pharmacy curriculum. Finally, given the size of the College of Pharmacy, which has about 35 full-time faculty, a two department system would be more in-keeping with other College structures on campus. The net loss of one chair in the College will result in the following annual savings: $3,000.00 chair supplement 1/9 to 3/9 of the contract salary for a summer salary. C. INSTITUTIONAL ROLE The merger is consistent with the University's efforts to promote efﬁciencies and increase productivity through restructuring. D. INTERINSTITUTIONAL CONSIDERATIONS None E. CONTENT No change in content F. Assessment of Student Learning Outcomes – University Manual

Assessment of Student Learning Outcomes
8.59.10 Assessment of student learning outcomes shall be coordinated by the Assistant Director of Student Learning, Outcomes Assessment and Accreditation (see 2.22.21 ) with the oversight of the JAPROA (see Sections 5.84.10 – 5.84.14). The following policies shall apply to this process: #23-24-7
8.59.11 Academic Program Engagement: All undergraduate, professional, and graduate academic programs, including General Education, shall be actively engaged in student learning outcomes assessment as evidenced by, but not limited to:
a) Published student learning outcomes that are clear statements of what students are expected to gain, achieve, demonstrate, or know at the completion of the academic program. These student learning outcomes shall be published on the program’s website as well as on the website for the Office of Student Learning, Outcomes Assessment, and Accreditation (SLOAA). These student learning outcomes shall be periodically reviewed by the academic program for ongoing relevance.

b) A plan of student learning outcomes assessment that is endorsed by the program’s faculty. Plans should include a regular and predictable cycle for collecting and analyzing assessment data, for discussing curricular and programmatic changes, for implementing interventions, and for re-assessing the impact of implemented changes. Outcomes assessment plans will be published on each program’s website as well as on the SLOAA website.
c) Reports of student learning outcomes assessment that are provided to SLOAA using staggered cycles of no more than 3 years. Cycles for accredited programs will be adjusted to decrease redundancy of effort. #09-10–29

8.59.12 SLOAA Guidance for Academic Programs: Guidelines and schedules for preparation of outcomes assessment plans and reports shall be provided by SLOAA with the assistance and approval of the Joint Committee on Academic Program Review and Outcomes Assessment (JAPROA). SLOAA shall offer advice on the logistics of collecting assessment data, support for analyzing the results, and feedback on designing curricular and programmatic changes. Rubrics for evaluating the plans and reports shall be generated by SLOAA and posted on its website. #09-10–29 #23-24-7
8.59.13 Evaluation of Plans and Reports: Student learning outcomes assessment plans and reports shall be submitted through SLOAA for evaluation and recommendations by JAPROA. Daniels I ask you to consider my candidacy for the Faculty Senate Executive Committee for a 2-year term, 2026-2028.
I am an associate professor of computer science, and will have been a member of the faculty for 10 years as of Fall 2026.
I am beginning my second term on the Faculty Senate, and just completing my first 1-year term on FSEC.
In my first term on Faculty Senate, I served two years as chair of the Committee on Technology and Infrastructure.
In that time, my primary focus was on developing consensus policies for ITS to replace unilaterally-developed policies set forth by the administration which hindered academic freedom, research, and teaching.
I have continued this effort as the FSEC liaison to CTI.
This has culminated in a draft of the new ITS policy (with several flaws noted by the faculty) presented for comment in the last month.

In my time on CTI and FSEC, I have served on the IT Governance committee, on the search committees for the Chief Information Officer as well as the University Librarian, and am a founding member of the ad-hoc committees to proactively evaluate whether the technologies on which we depend are effective before the administration signs lengthy contracts.
I enjoy bringing my own perspective to these intellectually diverse working groups, and reconciling that perspective with those of others.
I see the particular strengths I bring to FSEC as including a deep understanding of both technology and how people use technology, as well as a bulwark to efforts to corporatize university ITS and other aspects of university life.
In a tumultuous time when new cybersecurity threats lead to sometimes-draconian policies that can impact research and teaching, as well as the rise of “AI” everywhere (sometimes without the needed critical thinking), I believe I can bring expertise and reasoned argument to addressing these issues.
Beyond technology, I see the adoption of the new budget model and the recent, eye-opening budget committee survey as being a key concern of FSEC going forward.
I believe we must work with the administration to address specific concerns brought to light by that survey, outreach to faculty, and other data such as the explosion of new course proposals. 1
